Silence of God
sī´lĕns ŭv gŏd
n. phrase (the experience of praying and receiving no answer; God's hiddenness as Scripture itself describes it)
The Bible has no single term for this; it has a vocabulary of complaint — how long, why standest thou afar off, thou hearest not — and it puts that vocabulary in the mouths of its most faithful men, and into the Psalter for congregational use.

See also: Silence of God

Biblical Definition

The silence of God is a recorded experience of the faithful. David: “O my God, I cry in the daytime, but thou hearest not; and in the night season, and am not silent” (Psa 22:2). Again: “How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?” (Psa 13:1). Habakkuk opens his book with it: “O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!” (Hab 1:2). Job searches in every direction: “Behold, I go forward, but he is not there; and backward, but I cannot perceive him” (Job 23:8). And Isaiah says it of God without reproach: “Verily thou art a God that hidest thyself, O God of Israel, the Saviour” (Isa 45:15).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines silence as stillness; the state of a person or thing not speaking; and, of God, forbearance of speech; and hiddenness as the state of being concealed.

expand to see more

SILENCE, n. In a general sense, stillness, or entire absence of sound or noise.

2. The state of a person or thing not speaking; forbearance of speech in man.

3. Habitual taciturnity; opposed to loquacity.

4. Oblivion; obscurity.

HIDE, v.t. To conceal; to withhold or withdraw from sight.

Key Scripture

Psa 22:2 — "O my God, I cry in the daytime, but thou hearest not; and in the night season, and am not silent."

Psa 13:1 — "To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?"

Hab 1:2 — "O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear! even cry out unto thee of violence, and thou wilt not save!"

Job 23:8 — "Behold, I go forward, but he is not there; and backward, but I cannot perceive him:"

Isa 45:15 — "Verily thou art a God that hidest thyself, O God of Israel, the Saviour."

Modern Corruption

Silence is treated as evidence of God's absence or of the believer's failure, and Scripture gives it to its best men and puts their complaints in the hymnbook.

expand to see more

The first thing to say is that the complaint is canonical. Psalm 13 begins with four how longs and Psalm 22 with why hast thou forsaken me, and these were not private notes — they were given to the chief Musician, for public singing. A tradition that has no vocabulary for unanswered prayer has edited its own hymnbook, and it leaves sufferers with the impression that their experience is unusual and disgraceful when it is neither. Roughly a third of the Psalter is lament.

The second thing is what those psalms do with the silence, because they do not stay in it and they do not resolve it cheaply either. Psalm 13 turns at verse 5 — but I have trusted in thy mercy — without anything having changed in the circumstances. Psalm 22 moves from forsakenness to thou hast heard me and ends with the ends of the world remembering and turning to the LORD. Job 23 is the model of honest searching: he cannot find God in any direction, and in the same breath says, but he knoweth the way that I take: when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold.

The third thing is the one that finally answers it. Psalm 22:2 is quoted from the cross, and there the silence was real and total and undeserved: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? Whatever a believer experiences of God's hiddenness, it is not the abandonment Christ bore, and it is not the same thing because that one was. Hebrews says of Him that in the days of his flesh he offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears, and was heard — and the answer, that time, came after the grave. Isaiah 45:15 is the sober statement of the doctrine and it does not apologise: thou art a God that hidest thyself — and the same clause calls Him the Saviour.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ad-anah (H575), how long; sathar (H5641), to hide; azab (H5800), to forsake; Greek egkataleipo (G1459), to abandon.

expand to see more

Hebrew ad-anah (H575) — how long; Psalm 13:1–2, Habakkuk 1:2, Job 18:2, Exodus 16:28.

Hebrew sathar panim (H5641) — to hide the face; Psalm 13:1, 27:9, 88:14, Isaiah 45:15, 54:8.

Greek egkatelipes (G1459) — hast thou forsaken; Matthew 27:46, Mark 15:34, quoting Psalm 22:1.

Usage

"“I cry in the daytime, but thou hearest not” — given to the chief Musician."

"“He knoweth the way that I take” — said by a man who could not find Him."

"“Thou art a God that hidest thyself… the Saviour” — both, in one clause."
